stem: Thickness of the glass of a spectacle is 2 mm and refractive index of its glass is 1.5. Calculate time taken by light to cross this thickness. Express your answer with the most convenient prefix attached to the unit 'second'.
solution:
Speed of light in vacuum, \( c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \)
\( n_{glass} = 10.5 \)
\( \therefore \) Speed of light in glass \( = \dfrac{c}{n_{glass}} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \)
Distance to be travelled by light in glass, \( s = 2\ \text{mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} \)
\( \therefore \) Time \( t \) required by light to travel this distance,
\( t = \dfrac{s}{v_{glass}} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3}}{2 \times 10^{8}} = 10^{-11}\ \text{s} \)
Most convenient prefix to express this small time is pico (p) \( = 10^{-12} \)
\( \therefore t = 10 \times 10^{-12} = 10\ \text{ps} \)

subtopic: Reflection from Plane and Curved Mirrors
stem: A small object is kept symmetrically between two plane mirrors inclined at \( 38^\circ \). This angle is now gradually increased to \( 41^\circ \), the object being symmetrical all the time. Determine the number of images visible during the process.
solution:
According to the convention used in the table above,
\( \theta = 38^{0} \therefore n = \dfrac{360}{38} = 9.47 \)
\( \therefore N = 9 \). This is valid till the angle is \( 40^\circ \) as the object is kept symmetrically.
Beyond \( 40^\circ \), \( n < 9 \) and it decreases upto \( \dfrac{360}{41} = 8.78 \).
Hence now onwards there will be 8 images till \( 41^\circ \).

subtopic: Reflection from Plane and Curved Mirrors
stem: A thin pencil of length 20 cm is kept along the principal axis of a concave mirror of curvature 30 cm. Nearest end of the pencil is 20 cm from the pole of the mirror. What will be the size of image of the pencil?
solution:
\( R = 30\ \text{cm} \)
\( f = R/2 = -15\ \text{cm} \) ... (Concave mirror)
\( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} \)
For nearest end, \( u = u_{1} = -20\ \text{cm} \). Let the image distance be \( v_{1} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{-15} = \dfrac{1}{v_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{-20} \quad \therefore v_{1} = -60\ \text{cm} \)
Nearest end is at 20 cm and pencil itself is 20 cm long. Hence farthest end is \( 20 + 20 = 40\ \text{cm} = -u_{2} \)
Let the image distance be \( v_{2} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{-15} = \dfrac{1}{v_{2}} + \dfrac{1}{-40} \quad \therefore v_{2} = -24\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore \) Length of the image \( = 60 - 24 = 36\ \text{cm} \).

stem: A crane flying 6 m above a still, clear water lake sees a fish underwater. For the crane, the fish appears to be 6 cm below the water surface. How much deep should the crane immerse its beak to pick that fish? For the fish, how much above the water surface does the crane appear? Refractive index of water = 4/3.
solution:
For crane, apparent depth of the fish is 6 cm and real depth is to be determined.
For fish, real depth (height, in this case) of the crane is 6 m and apparent depth (height) is to be determined.
\( n = \dfrac{R}{A} = \dfrac{\text{Real depth}}{\text{Apparent depth}} \)
For crane, it is water with respect to air as real depth is in water and apparent depth is as seen from air
\( \therefore n = \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{R}{A} = \dfrac{R}{6} \quad \therefore R = 8\ \text{cm} \)
For fish, it is air with respect to water as the real height is in air and seen from water.
\( \therefore n = \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{R}{A} = \dfrac{6}{A} \quad \therefore A = 8\ \text{m} \)

stem: There is a tiny LED bulb at the center of the bottom of a cylindrical vessel of diameter 6 cm. Height of the vessel is 4 cm. The beaker is filled completely with an optically dense liquid. The bulb is visible from any inclined position but just visible if seen along the edge of the beaker. Determine refractive index of the liquid.
solution:
As seen from the accompanying figure, if the bulb is just visible from the edge, angle of incidence in the liquid (at the edge) must be the critical angle of incidence, \( i_{c} \). The bulb is at the centre of the base, so the horizontal distance to the edge is half the diameter, i.e. 3 cm, while the height of the liquid column is 4 cm.
From the dimensions given,
\( \tan(i_{c}) = \dfrac{3}{4} \quad \therefore \sin(i_{c}) = \dfrac{3}{5} \quad \therefore n_{liquid} = \dfrac{\sin 90^\circ}{\sin(i_{c})} = \dfrac{5}{3} \)

subtopic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
stem: A glass paper-weight \( (n = 1.5) \) of radius 3 cm has a tiny air bubble trapped inside it. Closest distance of the bubble from the surface is 2 cm. Where will it appear when seen from the other end (from where it is farthest)?
solution:
Accompanying figure illustrates the location of the bubble: the bubble lies on the diameter, 2 cm from the near surface, so it is \( 2 + 3 = 5 \) cm from the centre measured the other way and \( 3 + 1 = 4 \) cm from the far surface P through which it is viewed.
According to the symbols used in the Eq. (9.4), we get,
\( n_{1} = \) refractive index of the medium of real object (medium of incident rays) \( = 1.5 \)
\( n_{2} = \) refractive index of the other medium \( = 1 \)
\( u = -4\ \text{cm} \)
\( v = ? \)
\( R = -3\ \text{cm} \)
\( \dfrac{n_{2} - n_{1}}{R} = \dfrac{n_{2}}{v} - \dfrac{n_{1}}{u} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1 - 1.5}{-3} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1.5}{-4} \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{3}{8} \quad \therefore v = -4.8\ \text{cm} \)
In this case apparent depth is NOT less than real depth. This is due to curvature of the refracting surface.

subtopic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
stem: A dense glass double convex lens \( (n = 2) \) designed to reduce spherical aberration has \( |R_{1}| : |R_{2}| = 1 : 5 \). If a point object is kept 15 cm in front of this lens, it produces its real image at 7.5 cm. Determine \( R_{1} \) and \( R_{2} \).
solution:
\( u = -15\ \text{cm} \), \( v = +7.5\ \text{cm} \) (real image is on opposite side).
\( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{7.5} - \dfrac{1}{-15} \quad \therefore f = +5\ \text{cm} \)
The lens is double convex. Hence, \( R_{1} \) is positive and \( R_{2} \) is negative. Also, \( |R_{2}| = 5|R_{1}| \) and \( n = 2 \).
\( (n - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) = \dfrac{1}{f} \)
\( \therefore (2 - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{-(5R_{1})} \right) = \dfrac{1}{5} \)
\( \therefore (1)\left( \dfrac{6}{5R_{1}} \right) = \dfrac{1}{5} \quad \therefore R_{1} = 6\ \text{cm} \quad \therefore R_{2} = 30\ \text{cm} \)

stem: A fine beam of white light is incident upon the longer side of a plane parallel glass slab of breadth 5 cm at angle of incidence \( 60^{0} \). Calculate angular deviation of red and violet rays within the slab and lateral dispersion between them as they emerge from the opposite side. Refractive indices of the glass for red and violet are 1.51 and 1.53 respectively.
solution:
As shown in the Fig. 9.15 above, \( \text{VM} = L_{V} \) and \( \text{RT} = L_{R} \) give respective lateral deviations for violet and red colours and \( L_{VR} = L_{V} - L_{R} \) is the lateral dispersion between these colours. \( n_{R} = 1.51 \), \( n_{V} = 1.53 \) and \( i = 60^\circ \)
\( \therefore \sin r_{R} = \dfrac{\sin i}{n_{R}} = \dfrac{\sin 60^{0}}{1.51} = 0.5735 \)
\( \sin r_{V} = \dfrac{\sin i}{n_{V}} = \dfrac{\sin 60^{0}}{1.53} = 0.566 \)
\( \therefore r_{R} = 35^{0} \) and \( R_{V} = 34^{0}28' \quad \therefore \delta_{RV} = r_{R} - r_{V}\ 32' \)
\( \therefore i - r_{R} = 25^{0} \), \( i - r_{V} = 25^{0}32' \)
\( \therefore \text{AR} = \dfrac{\text{AN}}{\cos r_{R}} = 6.104\ \text{cm} \)
\( \text{AV} = \dfrac{\text{AN}}{\cos r_{V}} = 6.063\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore L_{R} = \text{RT} = \text{AR}\left( \sin[i - r_{R}] \right) = 2.58\ \text{cm} \)
\( L_{V} = \text{VM} = \text{AV}\left( \sin[i - r_{V}] \right) = 2.58\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore L_{VR} = L_{V} - L_{R} = 0.033\ \text{cm} = 0.33\ \text{mm} \)
It shows that the lateral dispersion is too small to detect.

stem: For a glass \( (n = 1.5) \) prism having refracting angle \( 60^{0} \), determine the range of angle of incidence for which emergent ray is possible from the opposite surface and the corresponding angles of emergence. Also calculate the angle of incidence for which \( i = e \). How much is the corresponding angle of minimum deviation?
solution:
As shown in the box above, \( i_{min} = 27^{0}55' \). Angle of emergence for this is \( e_{max} = 90^{0} \).
From the principle of reversibility of light, \( i_{max} = 90^{0} \) and \( e_{min} = 27^{0}55' \)
Also, from the box above,
\( n = \dfrac{\sin\left( \dfrac{60 + \delta_{m}}{2} \right)}{\sin\left( \dfrac{60}{2} \right)} = \dfrac{\sin\left( 30 + \dfrac{\delta_{m}}{2} \right)}{\sin(30)} = 2\sin\left( 30 + \dfrac{\delta_{m}}{2} \right) \)
\( \therefore 1.5 = 2\sin\left( 30 + \dfrac{\delta_{m}}{2} \right) \quad \therefore 0.75 = \sin\left( 30 + \dfrac{\delta_{m}}{2} \right) \)
\( \therefore \left( 30 + \dfrac{\delta_{m}}{2} \right) = 48^{0}35' \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{\delta_{m}}{2} = 18^{0}35' \quad \therefore \delta_{m} = 37^{0}10' \)
\( i + e = A + \delta \) and \( i = e \) for \( \delta = \delta_{m} \)
\( \therefore i + i = 60 + 37^\circ 10' = 97^\circ 10' \quad \therefore i = 48^\circ 35' \)

stem: For a dense flint glass prism of refracting angle \( 10^{0} \), obtain angular deviation for extreme colours and dispersive power of dense flint glass. \( (n_{red} = 1.712,\ n_{violet} = 1.792) \)
solution:
\( \delta_{V} = A(n_{V} - 1) = 10(1.792 - 1) = (7.92)^\circ \)
\( \delta_{R} = A(n_{R} - 1) = 10(1.712 - 1) = (7.12)^\circ \)
\( \therefore \) Angular dispersion, \( \delta_{VR} = \delta_{V} - \delta_{R} = (0.8)^{0} \)
dispersive power, \( \omega = \dfrac{\delta_{V} - \delta_{R}}{\left( \dfrac{\delta_{V} + \delta_{R}}{2} \right)} = 2\left( \dfrac{7.92 - 7.12}{7.92 + 7.12} \right) = \dfrac{2 \times 0.8}{15.04} = 0.1064 \)
(This is much higher than popular crown glass)

stem: After Cataract operation, a person is recommended with concavo-convex spectacles of curvatures 10 cm and 50 cm. Crown glass of refractive indices 1.51 for red and 1.53 for violet colours is used for this. Calculate the lateral chromatic aberration occurring due to these glasses.
solution:
For a concavo-concave lens, both the radii of curvature are either positive or both negative. If convex shape faces object, both will be positive. See the accompanying figure.
\( \therefore R_{1} = 10\ \text{cm} \) and \( R_{2} = 50\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore \left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) = \left( \dfrac{1}{+10} - \dfrac{1}{+50} \right) = 0.08\ \text{cm}^{-1} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{f_{R}} = (n_{R} - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) = (1.51 - 1) \times 0.08 = 0.0408 \quad \therefore f_{R} = 25.51\ \text{cm} \)
and \( \dfrac{1}{f_{V}} = (n_{V} - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) = (1.53 - 1) \times 0.08 = 0.0424 \quad \therefore f_{V} = 23.58\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore \) Longitudinal chromatic aberration \( = f_{V} - f_{R} = 25.51 - 23.58 = 1.93\ \text{cm} \), ... (quite appreciable!)
Verify that you get the same answer even if you consider the concave surface facing the incident rays.

stem: A magnifying glass of focal length 10 cm is used to read letters of thickness 0.5 mm held 8 cm away from the lens. Calculate the image size. How big will the letters appear? Can you read the letters if held 5 cm away from the lens? If yes, of what size would the letters appear? If no, why not?
solution:
\( f = +10\ \text{cm},\ u = -8\ \text{cm},\ v = ? \)
\( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{-8} \quad \therefore v = -40\ \text{cm} \)
\( m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{\text{Image size } h_{i}}{\text{Object size } h_{o}} \quad \therefore \dfrac{40}{8} = \dfrac{h_{i}}{0.5} \)
\( \therefore h_{i} = 2.5\ \text{cm} \) (5 times that of the object)
\( M = \dfrac{D}{u} = \dfrac{25}{8} = 3.125 \)
\( \therefore \) Image will appear to be 3.125 times bigger. i.e., \( 3.125 \times 0.5 = 1.5625\ \text{cm} \)
For \( \mu = -5\ \text{cm} \), \( v \) will be \( -10\ \text{cm} \).
For an average human being to see clearly, the image must be at or beyond 25 cm. Thus, it will not possible to read the letters if held 5 cm away from the lens.

stem: The pocket microscope used by a student consists of eye lens of focal length 6.25 cm and objective of focal length 2 cm. At microscope length 15 cm, the final image appears biggest. Estimate distance of the object from the objective and magnifying power of the microscope.
solution:
\( f_{e} = 6.25\ \text{cm},\ f_{o} = 2\ \text{cm},\ L = |v_{o}| + |u_{e}| = 15\ \text{cm},\ v_{e} = 25\ \text{cm} \) (Image appears largest)
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{v_{e}} - \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{6.25} = \dfrac{4}{25} = \dfrac{1}{-25} - \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} \quad \therefore |u_{e}| = 5\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore |v_{o}| = L - |u_{e}| = 15 - 5 = 10\ \text{cm} \)
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{o}} = \dfrac{1}{v_{o}} - \dfrac{1}{u_{o}} \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{+10} - \dfrac{1}{u_{o}} \quad \therefore |u_{o}| = 2.5\ \text{cm} \)
\( M = m_{o} \times M_{e} = \left( \dfrac{v_{o}}{u_{o}} \right)\left( \dfrac{D}{u_{e}} \right) = \left( \dfrac{10}{2.5} \right)\left( \dfrac{25}{5} \right) = 4 \times 5 = 20 \)

stem: Focal length of the objective of an astronomical telescope is 1 m. Under normal adjustment, length of the telescope is 1.05 m. Calculate focal length of the eyepiece and magnifying power under normal adjustment.
solution:
For astronomical telescope,
\( L = f_{0} + f_{e} \quad \therefore 1.05 = 1 + f_{0} \quad \therefore f_{e} = 0.05\ \text{m} = 5\ \text{cm} \)
Under normal adjustments,
\( M = \dfrac{f_{o}}{f_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{0.05} = 20 \)
